August 17, 2026 Badlan (Day 6) Underworld-Badland ALE-IB Free-Surface Modeling Lu et al., 2026 (GMD)

Focus: Interpretation of two related Lu et al. papers and their implications for developing a scientific manuscript and numerical experiments with the ASPECT–Landlab coupling framework.

The two papers are best viewed as a progression:

\[\boxed{ \text{true free surface} \rightarrow \text{surface-process coupling} \rightarrow \text{tectonic--landscape feedback} }\]

The first paper establishes the numerical foundation: a true free-surface treatment using an Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian scheme with an internal boundary (ALE-IB). The second extends the framework to coupling tectonic deformation with erosion and deposition.

The two papers are:

  • Lu, N., Moresi, L., and Giordani, J. (2026). A novel ALE scheme with the internal boundary for true free surface simulation in geodynamic models. Geoscientific Model Development, 19, 5191–5206. DOI: 10.5194/gmd-19-5191-2026.

  • Lu, N., Moresi, L., Giordani, J., and Knight, B. S. (2026). A novel ALE scheme with the internal boundary for coupling tectonic and surface processes in geodynamic models. Geoscientific Model Development, 19, 5723–5741. DOI: 10.5194/gmd-19-5723-2026.

Two-paper conceptual progression

Table 14 Scientific progression

Paper

Main numerical problem

Relevance to ASPECT–Landlab

Lu et al. (2026a)

Stable and accurate true free-surface evolution

Surface motion, mesh deformation, stability, validation

Lu et al. (2026b)

Coupling tectonic deformation with erosion and deposition

Two-way tectonic–landscape coupling

The first paper asks:

Can we accurately move the geodynamic free surface?

The second asks:

What happens when a moving free surface is simultaneously modified by tectonic deformation and surface processes?

For ASPECT–Landlab, the natural next question is:

How accurately and efficiently can a finite-element geodynamic model exchange deformation with a raster landscape-evolution model, and how does the numerical coupling itself influence erosion, transport, and deposition?

1. Lu et al. (2026a): True free-surface simulation

Scientific motivation

Traditional geodynamic models often use simplified upper boundary conditions such as free-slip or no-slip. These do not explicitly allow the Earth’s surface to deform as a physical free surface.

The sticky-air approach can represent topography but introduces additional computational volume and can suffer from marker fluctuations and the drunken sailor or sloshing instability.

The central contribution is:

\[\boxed{\text{ALE--IB = ALE + internal boundary}}\]

The internal boundary represents the true free surface inside the computational domain while retaining an upper sticky-air-like region.

Core free-surface update

The free surface is represented by mesh nodes on \(\Gamma_{\rm fs}\):

\[\mathbf{X}^{n+1} = \mathbf{X}^{n} + \Delta t\,\mathbf{u}^{n} \qquad \text{on } \Gamma_{\rm fs}.\]

This expresses the basic relation:

\[\text{surface displacement} = \text{surface velocity} \times \text{time interval}.\]

Free-surface update sequence

The numerical workflow can be summarized as:

Solve Stokes equations
          |
          v
    Obtain velocity
          |
          v
    Advect free surface
          |
          v
    Resample surface
          |
          v
    Solve Laplace equation
          |
          v
    Propagate mesh displacement
          |
          v
    Update / remesh mesh
          |
          v
    Continue simulation

The mesh displacement is obtained from:

\[\nabla^2 D_z = 0.\]

The important point for ASPECT–Landlab is that surface deformation must be propagated into the computational mesh while preserving mesh quality.

Free-surface stabilization

Lu et al. investigate a Free Surface Stabilization Algorithm (FSSA) and timestep convergence. This is directly relevant to our n_substeps work.

Two different numerical questions should be separated:

  1. Is the free-surface update itself stable?

  2. How frequently should the surface-process operator interact with the geodynamic operator?

These are related but distinct numerical problems.

Numerical experiments

The first paper considers:

  • sinusoidal topography relaxation;

  • Rayleigh–Taylor instability;

  • delamination;

  • rising sphere;

  • subduction.

The sinusoidal relaxation case is especially useful for ASPECT–Landlab because an analytical solution is available:

\[w(x,t) = w(x,0)\exp\left(-\frac{t}{t^*}\right).\]

This provides a clean validation problem.

The paper also shows that higher-order elements can improve accuracy and that ALE-IB is robust for strongly asymmetric geometries.

2. Lu et al. (2026b): Coupling tectonics and surface processes

The second paper extends the free-surface framework to tectonic–surface coupling.

The surface evolution equation is:

\[\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = U - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}_r - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}_d,\]

where \(h\) is surface elevation, \(U\) is tectonic uplift, \(\mathbf{q}_r\) is fluvial sediment flux, and \(\mathbf{q}_d\) is hillslope sediment flux.

For ASPECT–Landlab this can be interpreted as:

\[\boxed{ \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = u_z - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}_{surface} }\]

Coupling sequence

The second paper’s coupling workflow is:

  1. Solve the Stokes equations.

  2. Obtain the velocity field.

  3. Evaluate velocity on the surface.

  4. Transfer velocity to the surface-process model.

  5. Evolve the landscape through erosion and deposition.

  6. Transfer the modified surface back to the tectonic model.

  7. Remesh the tectonic domain.

  8. Continue the simulation.

This is conceptually very close to the ASPECT–Landlab architecture.

Two surfaces

The paper distinguishes between:

\[T\text{-surface} = \text{tectonic-model surface}\]

and:

\[S\text{-surface} = \text{surface-process-model surface}.\]

The conceptual exchange is:

ASPECT
   |
   | velocity
   v
T-surface
   |
   | transfer
   v
Landlab
   |
   | erosion/deposition
   v
S-surface
   |
   | transfer back
   v
ASPECT surface

3. Relevance to the ASPECT–Landlab implementation

The major difference from the UWGeodynamics–Badlands implementation is the spatial-transfer mechanism.

For ASPECT-to-Landlab transfer, the finite-element solution can be evaluated at Landlab points using deal.II RemotePointEvaluation.

For the reverse direction, the closest Landlab point can be assigned to an ASPECT surface degree of freedom:

\[j^*(i) = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_j \left\| \mathbf{x}_i^A-\mathbf{x}_j^L \right\|^2,\]

followed by:

\[\mathbf{u}_i^A = \mathbf{u}_{j^*(i)}^L.\]

Therefore, the current ASPECT–Landlab coupling is spatially asymmetric.

Table 15 Spatial transfer comparison

Coupling

Direction

Transfer

UWGeo dynamics–Badlands

Underworld -> surface

Cubic spline interpolation

ASPECT–Landlab

ASPECT -> Landlab

FE point evaluation

ASPECT–Landlab

Landlab -> ASPECT

Closest-point assignment

This difference should be explicitly documented in a future manuscript.

4. Connection to the current n_substeps investigation

The second Lu et al. paper divides the tectonic timestep into smaller surface-process timesteps. This directly connects to our n_substeps investigation.

Let:

\[\Delta t_{\rm sub} = \frac{\Delta t}{N}.\]

Then total tectonic displacement remains:

\[\sum_{k=1}^{N} U\,\Delta t_{\rm sub} = N U \frac{\Delta t}{N} = U\Delta t.\]

Therefore, changing n_substeps does not necessarily change the total tectonic uplift. If the final landscape changes, the difference can instead result from the frequency of interaction between tectonic and landscape operators.

The coupling can be represented as:

\[\mathcal{I}_{A\rightarrow L} \rightarrow \mathcal{E}_{L} \rightarrow \mathcal{I}_{L\rightarrow A}.\]

The central numerical question becomes:

How does the frequency of tectonic–surface-process coupling affect the accuracy and convergence of landscape evolution?

This connects the current n_substeps work directly to the literature.

5. What should be reproduced in ASPECT–Landlab?

Topographic relaxation

A first experiment should reproduce the sinusoidal relaxation problem.

Possible tests include:

  • free-surface evolution;

  • hillslope diffusion;

  • fluvial incision;

  • erosion and deposition;

  • sediment redistribution;

  • comparison against an analytical solution.

A useful parameter sweep is:

\[k_f = 0,\, 10^{-6},\, 10^{-5},\, 10^{-4}\]

with a representative hillslope diffusion coefficient.

The purpose is not simply to reproduce the paper, but to establish a controlled benchmark for the ASPECT–Landlab coupling.

Fluvial erodibility

Increasing fluvial erodibility should be examined through:

  • incision depth;

  • longitudinal profile shape;

  • relief;

  • drainage-network development;

  • erosion rate;

  • deposition rate.

This provides a controlled Landlab sensitivity experiment.

Continental collision

A collision experiment can investigate:

\[\text{convergence} \rightarrow \text{shortening} \rightarrow \text{crustal thickening} \rightarrow \text{mountain building} \rightarrow \text{erosion} \rightarrow \text{sediment transport/deposition}.\]

This represents an actively forced tectonic experiment rather than a purely numerical benchmark.

6. What the papers leave open

The papers provide a strong foundation but leave several opportunities for ASPECT–Landlab.

  1. The numerical consequences of different coupling frequencies are not the central focus.

  2. Spatial resolution mismatch between the tectonic and landscape grids is not systematically explored.

  3. The consequences of different transfer strategies deserve quantitative investigation.

  4. The coupled framework can be extended toward more explicit sediment routing and storage.

  5. A rift setting, with simultaneous uplift and subsidence, provides a useful complementary application to collision.

7. Proposed manuscript direction

The manuscript should not simply state:

We coupled ASPECT with Landlab.

A stronger manuscript would ask a numerical-scientific question about the coupling.

Possible titles include:

Numerical accuracy and coupling-frequency effects in two-way ASPECT–Landlab simulations of tectonic surface evolution

or:

From tectonic deformation to sediment redistribution: numerical assessment of two-way ASPECT–Landlab coupling

The manuscript can be organized into three levels.

Level 1: Numerical verification

Test whether ASPECT–Landlab reproduces a known free-surface solution.

Use sinusoidal relaxation and measure:

\[E_{L_2} = \left[ \frac{ \sum_i (h_i^{\rm numerical}-h_i^{\rm analytical})^2 }{ \sum_i (h_i^{\rm analytical})^2 } \right]^{1/2}.\]

Also measure:

  • maximum topographic error;

  • RMSE;

  • phase error;

  • free-surface displacement;

  • erosion/deposition error.

Level 2: Coupling verification

Add Landlab surface processes and compare:

Table 16 Suggested coupling cases

Case

Tectonic component

Landlab component

TR-TM

None

TR-D

ASPECT

Hillslope diffusion

Potential applications include:

8. Why a rift experiment may be particularly powerful —————————————————————————–===

A collision model is useful, but a rift experiment may provide a more distinct scientific application for ASPECT–Landlab.

In a collision:

\[\text{convergence} \rightarrow \text{uplift} \rightarrow \text{erosion}.\]

A rift produces both uplift and subsidence:

\[U_{\rm tectonic}(x,y,t)=u_z(x,y,t),\]

with:

\[U_{\rm tectonic}>0 \qquad \text{uplift}\]

and:

\[U_{\rm tectonic}<0 \qquad \text{subsidence}.\]

The landscape therefore contains simultaneous sediment sources and sinks.

The full feedback can be:

\[\boxed{ \text{extension} \rightarrow \text{faulting} \rightarrow \text{uplift/subsidence} \rightarrow \text{erosion/deposition} \rightarrow \text{sediment loading} \rightarrow \text{tectonic response} }\]

A possible rift question is:

How does sediment redistribution modify the topographic and tectonic evolution of an actively deforming rift system?

9. Sediment routing as a longer-term opportunity

The Lu et al. framework primarily represents surface processes through fluvial and hillslope terms.

A more ambitious ASPECT–Landlab model could explicitly track sediment:

\[\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = U - \nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}_s,\]

where \(\mathbf{q}_s\) is sediment flux.

Distinguish sediment supply:

\[Q_s=\text{sediment supply}\]

from transport capacity:

\[Q_t=\text{transport capacity}.\]

If:

\[Q_s < Q_t,\]

sediment can continue to move downstream.

If:

\[Q_s > Q_t,\]

the excess sediment is deposited.

Conceptually:

\[Q_{\rm dep} \sim Q_s-Q_t \qquad \text{when } Q_s>Q_t.\]

This moves the framework from a simple erosion model toward a source-to-sink sediment-routing model.

10. Central research question

The strongest central question from today’s discussion is:

\[\boxed{ \text{How does the numerical coupling between tectonic deformation and landscape evolution control the predicted evolution of topography, erosion, and sediment deposition?} }\]

This can be divided into three questions.

Question 1: Spatial coupling

How does the mismatch between the ASPECT finite-element discretization and the Landlab raster grid affect transferred tectonic velocity and landscape evolution?

\[\mathbf{u}_{ASPECT} \rightarrow \mathbf{u}_{Landlab}.\]

Important parameters include:

  • ASPECT mesh resolution;

  • Landlab resolution;

  • relative grid alignment;

  • transfer method;

  • sharpness of tectonic deformation.

Question 2: Temporal coupling

How does n_substeps affect the numerical solution?

The working hypothesis is:

\[\boxed{ \text{Increasing coupling frequency reduces temporal operator-splitting error} }\]

A useful test is:

n_substeps =
    1
    2
    3
    5
    10
    20
    40
    80

Measure:

  • final topography;

  • maximum erosion;

  • maximum deposition;

  • cumulative erosion;

  • cumulative deposition;

  • sediment flux;

  • drainage-network metrics.

Question 3: Physical coupling

How does erosion and deposition feed back onto tectonic deformation?

\[\text{tectonic deformation} \rightarrow \text{topography} \rightarrow \text{erosion} \rightarrow \text{sediment redistribution} \rightarrow \text{surface loading} \rightarrow \text{tectonic response}.\]

12. Numerical convergence experiment

Define a reference solution:

\[h_{\rm ref}=h_{N_{\rm ref}},\]

where, for example,

\[N_{\rm ref}=40 \quad\text{or}\quad 80.\]

Then calculate:

\[E_h(N) = \left[ \frac{1}{A} \int_A \left( h_N-h_{\rm ref} \right)^2 dA \right]^{1/2}.\]

Similarly:

\[E_E(N)=\left|E_N-E_{\rm ref}\right|\]

and:

\[E_D(N)=\left|D_N-D_{\rm ref}\right|.\]

The key analysis is whether numerical error decreases toward a converged solution as n_substeps increases.

13. Spatial versus temporal coupling error

We should explicitly distinguish two types of coupling error.

Spatial coupling error:

\[E_{\rm spatial} = f( \Delta x_A, \Delta x_L, \text{grid alignment}, \text{transfer method} ).\]

Temporal coupling error:

\[E_{\rm temporal} = f( \Delta t, n_{\rm substeps} ).\]

Therefore:

\[\boxed{ E_{\rm total} = E_{\rm spatial} + E_{\rm temporal} + E_{\rm physical} }\]

where E_physical represents differences caused by changes in the physical parameterization rather than numerical coupling.

Separating these error sources could make the manuscript substantially stronger.

15. What would make the manuscript genuinely new?

The manuscript should avoid presenting the contribution as merely:

ASPECT + Landlab coupling

because the general concept of coupling geodynamics and landscape evolution already exists.

The novelty should instead come from one or more of:

  1. A different coupling architecture

    ASPECT finite-element point evaluation + Landlab raster surface evolution.

  2. A quantitative study of spatial-transfer error

    Especially the consequences of asymmetric ASPECT-to-Landlab and Landlab-to-ASPECT transfer.

  3. A quantitative study of temporal coupling

    n_substeps as a control on operator-splitting error.

  4. A systematic sediment-routing experiment

    Moving beyond simple erosion/deposition to explicit sediment transport.

  5. A new tectonic setting

    For example, a rift where uplift and subsidence coexist.

  6. A numerical convergence framework

    Demonstrating when the coupled solution becomes insensitive to grid resolution and coupling frequency.

16. Recommended manuscript hypothesis

The most testable hypothesis is:

\[\boxed{ \text{The predicted landscape and sediment distribution in a two-way ASPECT--Landlab simulation depend systematically on both spatial-transfer resolution and temporal coupling frequency.} }\]

A more specific version is:

\[\boxed{ \text{As }n_{\rm substeps}\text{ increases, the coupled solution approaches a converged tectonic--landscape state, but the convergence rate depends on spatial resolution and the transfer method between ASPECT and Landlab.} }\]

18. Key conclusions from today’s discussion

The two Lu et al. papers provide a useful roadmap for ASPECT–Landlab.

First, Lu et al. (2026a) establishes that accurate free-surface evolution requires careful treatment of mesh motion, surface advection, and timestep stability.

Second, Lu et al. (2026b) demonstrates that when surface processes are coupled to tectonic deformation, numerical differences in surface tracking can propagate into erosion and sediment distribution.

Third, the ASPECT–Landlab coupling is numerically distinct from the Underworld–Badlands implementation because ASPECT-to-Landlab uses finite-element point evaluation, while the reverse transfer uses closest-point assignment.

Fourth, this asymmetric spatial transfer creates a natural numerical research problem.

Fifth, the current n_substeps investigation provides an equally important temporal numerical problem: how frequently the tectonic and landscape operators exchange information.

The coupled problem can therefore be summarized as:

\[\boxed{ \underbrace{ \mathcal{I}_{A\rightarrow L} }_{\text{spatial transfer}} \rightarrow \underbrace{ \mathcal{E}_{Landlab} }_{\text{surface evolution}} \rightarrow \underbrace{ \mathcal{I}_{L\rightarrow A} }_{\text{spatial transfer}} \rightarrow \underbrace{ \mathcal{S}_{ASPECT} }_{\text{tectonic evolution}} }\]

with:

\[\Delta t_{\rm sub} = \frac{\Delta t_{\rm ASPECT}} {n_{\rm substeps}}.\]

19. Central question to carry forward

Key research question

How do spatial and temporal errors in the two-way ASPECT–Landlab coupling propagate into predicted topography, erosion, sediment transport, and deposition during tectonic landscape evolution?

This naturally leads to:

\[\boxed{ \text{spatial transfer} \rightarrow \text{temporal coupling} \rightarrow \text{landscape/sediment response} }\]

The long-term scientific extension is:

\[\boxed{ \text{tectonics} \leftrightarrow \text{topography} \leftrightarrow \text{erosion} \leftrightarrow \text{sediment transport} \leftrightarrow \text{deposition} }\]

This moves the ASPECT–Landlab framework toward a genuinely coupled tectonic–landscape–sedimentary system.
